extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and educated readers interested in the nature and philosophy of mathematical work
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic treatment of what constitutes intellectual work in mathematics: its relation to empirical sciences, the role and changing standards of rigor, and how mathematicians respond to foundational crises. Intended to explain characteristics and norms of mathematical practice rather than give technical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of experiential familiarity to understand mathematical work
rubrics_metrics.description: A discussion of the nature of intellectual effort is difficult unless it presupposes an easy, routine familiarity with that field; it is exceptional to acquire understanding of a process without having previously acquired deep familiarity with running it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing or evaluating accounts of mathematical work requires active experience doing mathematics; lack of hands-on practice leads to superficial commentary, inability to properly document points, and flawed conclusions. Anti-pattern: attempting a non-technical account without experiential grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics' peculiar relationship to the natural sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The most vitally characteristic fact about mathematics is its quite peculiar relationship to the natural sciences, or more generally to any science which interprets experience on a higher than purely descriptive level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical endeavors by their links to empirical sciences: many inspirations come from science (geometry began as empirical), and mathematics pervades theoretical divisions of the natural sciences. A science's progress is often measured by how amenable it becomes to mathematical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which a field is amenable to mathematical method as criterion of success
rubrics_metrics.description: In modern empirical sciences it has become more and more a major criterion of success whether they have become accessible to the mathematical method or to the near-mathematical methods of physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging scientific or intellectual work, consider the extent to which problems and theories have been rendered tractable by mathematical formulation; increasing 'mathematization' (biology→chemistry→physics) is seen as scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of mathematical rigor (concept of exact proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the early twentieth century some mathematicians proposed that the concept of mathematical rigor—of what constitutes an exact proof—should be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor is not immutable; standards can be contested and redefined (e.g., intuitionistic demands). When producing mathematics, be explicit about which standard of rigor is being used and aware that different communities may accept different notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitionistic critique vs everyday practice (trespassing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few mathematicians were willing to accept the new, exigent standards for daily use; many admitted the intuitionistic critique was prima facie right yet continued to 'trespass'—do mathematics in the old, easier fashion hoping others would justify it later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the common pragmatic gap between philosophical/technical critiques of foundations and the day-to-day methods mathematicians employ. Anti-pattern: claiming allegiance to a stricter foundational view while continuing to use the older methods without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's program for justifying classical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert proposed to justify classical mathematics by showing within an intuitionistic system how classical procedures operate and, ideally, proving intuitionistically that classical procedures cannot lead to contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating foundational programs, distinguish between describing how a system operates and proving its consistency; Hilbert's idea was to give an account of classical methods inside a constructive framework and then prove their safety—an ambitious methodological standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication of Gödel's result for foundational certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Gödel's essential import: if a system of mathematics does not lead into contradiction, then this fact cannot be demonstrated with the procedures of that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the methodological consequence that certain hopes for internal consistency proofs (as in Hilbert's program) are unattainable; one should be cautious about claims that a system can self-justify its absolute reliability. Use this as a criterion to temper expectations about foundational programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic justification: elegance and usefulness as grounds for acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: After foundational hopes faded, most mathematicians decided to use the classical system anyway because it produced results that were both elegant and useful; such practical success served as a justification comparable to accepting scientific theories like the electron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating mathematics, consider practical fruits—elegance and usefulness—as legitimate grounds for adopting methods even if absolute foundational justification is lacking. Scoring note: productivity and explanatory power can outweigh unresolved foundational concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against taking mathematical rigor as immovable
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of the foundational controversy is the best caution against taking the immovable rigor of mathematics too much for granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be humble and open to changes in standards; do not assume current notions of rigor are permanent truths. Reflective practice: reassess standards in light of new philosophical or technical developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of non-technical discussions of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A discussion of the nature of intellectual effort in mathematics kept on a non-mathematical plane will necessarily show some very bad features: points cannot be properly documented and an overall superficiality becomes unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evaluative or expository work about mathematics, prefer technical precision when possible; if constrained to non-technical exposition, acknowledge limitations, avoid overclaiming, and expect reduced ability to document detailed arguments.
